newsitem.title: USA: U.S. anti-missile system fails crucial test flight.
newsitem.headline: U.S. anti-missile system fails crucial test flight.

text.p: An advanced missile designed to protect U.S. troops and allies from missile attacks in a war suffered its fourth test failure on Thursday at White Sands, New Mexico, the U.S. Defence Department said.
Officials said it was too early to assess whether the failure would change plans to put the first of the Theatre High Altitude Area Defence (THAAD) missile systems into operation in 2004 as planned.
"We haven't heard anything about scrapping THAAD," said Sandra Trousdale, spokeswoman for the U.S. Army Missile Command. "Hopefully we'll have four more tries."

The missile system was scheduled to make 11 test flights at the desert range in southern New Mexico, but high-ranking army officials have said the success of Thursday's flight would be crucial in determining if it would be scrapped.
"That's a decision that will come down from way up, and it'll probably take some time," Trousdale said.
In the latest failed test, the THAAD missile was supposed to soar 100 feet (30 metres) high before striking down another missile launched a few minutes later from the other side of the range.
Trousdale said a preliminary investigation determined the THAAD missile locked onto the target with its radar but failed to intercept it.

The THAAD missile was designed to shoot down enemy missiles much higher and farther from U.S. troops and allied cities than Patriot missiles did in the Gulf War so debris would not fall on the targets as it did then.

Defence officials blamed the first test failure on an error in computer-guidance software, the second on a malfunction after booster missile separation and the third on an apparent electrical short that prevented the missile from locking on to its target.
